nameStory: This grasshopper earned its "pine tree" name because it's often found hopping among pine needles and branches, blending in with the dappled light of coniferous forests. The "spur-throat" part comes from a small spike-like projection on its throat, which looks like a tiny spur you might find on a cowboy boot.
description: The Pine Tree Spur-throat Grasshopper is a medium-sized hopper that loves hanging out in and around pine trees throughout New England. Like other grasshoppers, it has powerful hind legs built for jumping, short antennae, and wings that fold neatly along its back. Adults typically measure about an inch long and come in mottled brown and gray colors that help them disappear against tree bark and fallen pine needles. They're part of the large spur-throated grasshopper family, which includes many of our most common hoppers.

idTips.label: Throat Spur
idTips.description: Look for a small, pointed projection on the throat between the front legs - it feels firm and sharp to the touch, like a tiny thorn

idTips.label: Pine Association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near pine trees, often clinging to rough bark or resting on resinous branches that smell of pine pitch

idTips.label: Mottled Coloring
idTips.description: Brown and gray patches create a bark-like camouflage pattern that feels slightly rough when gently touched

idTips.label: Short Antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thick and shorter than the body, feeling sturdy rather than thread-like when carefully examined

idTips.label: Wing Length
idTips.description: Wings extend to about the tip of the abdomen, making a papery rustling sound when the grasshopper moves

habitat: Look for Pine Tree Spur-throat Grasshoppers in pine forests, mixed coniferous woodlands, and areas where white pines, red pines, or pitch pines grow throughout New England. They prefer the dappled sunlight of forest edges and clearings where pine trees meet meadows or roadsides. You'll often find them on pine bark, among fallen needles, or on low shrubs growing beneath pine canopies.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active; eggs are still developing in the soil among pine needle litter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most visible, actively feeding on pine needles and other vegetation, and easiest to spot and identify.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, mating and laying eggs in the soil before the first hard frosts end their season.
seasonality.winter: No visible activity; the species overwinters as eggs buried in soil beneath pine trees.

funFact: Despite being called a "pine tree" grasshopper, these hoppers can actually digest pine needles - something that would make most other insects sick due to the toxic resin compounds that pines use to defend themselves from herbivores.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other brown Melanoplus grasshoppers, but the pine tree association is your best clue - if you find a spur-throated grasshopper actually ON a pine tree rather than just in a meadow, you've likely found your species. Memory trick: "Pine plus spine" (the throat spur) equals pine tree grasshopper.
compareHints: Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Pine Tree Spur-throat stands out for its strong association with coniferous trees, while most others prefer grasses and herbs in open meadows. The Two-striped Grasshopper has obvious stripes and avoids trees, the Red-legged Grasshopper shows bright red on its hind legs, and the Differential Grasshopper is much larger and found in agricultural areas. The pine habitat preference makes this species fairly distinctive within the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Melanoplus relatives in New England, the two-striped grasshopper is the only one with those distinctive twin pale stripes running down its back.

Among its Melanoplus relatives, the red-legged grasshopper is distinguished primarily by those characteristic red-orange hind legs, while the two-striped grasshopper has prominent light stripes down its back, and the differential grasshopper is noticeably larger with chevron markings on its hind legs.
Among its Melanoplus relatives, the differential grasshopper is distinguished by its larger, more robust build and those characteristic dark leg markings.

Among its Melanoplus relatives, the Huckleberry Spur-throat is most reliably separated by habitat - Red-legged Grasshoppers prefer more open grassy areas, Two-striped Grasshoppers like agricultural fields, and Pine tree Spur-throats stick to coniferous areas.
